dropped.label: http-default-client-no-timeout
dropped.reason: ReadFromHTTP builds its client from http.DefaultClient (openapi3/loader_uri_reader.go:46), which has no Timeout and follows redirects. That is one facet of the same unbounded outbound-fetch surface as the $ref finding, and it has the same owner and the same fix location, so reporting it twice would double-count one control gap.

dropped.label: uri-cache-never-evicts
dropped.reason: URIMapCache (openapi3/loader_uri_reader.go:90-116) keeps every fetched URI's bytes in a map with no eviction and is what DefaultReadFromURI installs for every Loader. It only becomes reachable memory growth once external refs are enabled, which is the precondition of the $ref finding, so it is recorded there as a second consequence rather than as a separate item.

dropped.label: multipart-unbounded-part-count
dropped.reason: MultipartBodyDecoder (openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go:1489-1565) loops over mr.NextPart() with no part-count cap and accumulates every decoded part in `values`. The memory it consumes is proportional to the bytes actually received, so it is the same missing request-size bound as the body-buffering finding rather than an amplifier of its own.

dropped.label: query-array-split-on-empty-delimiter
dropped.reason: urlValuesDecoder.DecodeArray leaves `delim` as the empty string for any query style other than form/spaceDelimited/pipeDelimited, and strings.Split(v, "") would then produce one element per rune - an amplifier of roughly 50 bytes of heap per input byte. It is unreachable: Parameter.Validate rejects every other style for `in: query`, and both routers document that they assume a validated document.

dropped.label: loader-ref-cycle-recursion
dropped.reason: A document whose $refs form a cycle could drive resolveSchemaRef/resolvePathItemRef into unbounded recursion. It cannot: every resolver calls shouldVisitRef before recursing, which returns false when the ref string is already in loader.visitedRefs and instead queues a backtrack callback. Schema.validate carries the same protection independently via `slices.Contains(stack, schema)` at openapi3/schema.go:1397.

dropped.label: discriminator-mapping-nil-deref
dropped.reason: resolveDiscriminatorRef returns `discriminatorRef.Ref` from the else branch of a map lookup, which reads like a nil dereference whenever Discriminator.Mapping is empty or the key is absent. It is not: Mapping is StringMap[MappingRef], and StringMap[V] is declared as map[string]V - a value type, not a pointer - so the failed lookup yields a zero MappingRef struct and `.Ref` is the empty string.

findings.title: An array index taken verbatim from a query parameter name sizes a slice allocation (memory exhaustion)

location.component: openapi3filter: sliceMapToSlice and buildResObj, reached from urlValuesDecoder.DecodeObject

findings.evidence: Source is the raw HTTP query string, traced rather than assumed: RequestValidationInput.GetQueryParams returns input.Request.URL.Query() (openapi3filter/validate_request_input.go:31-37), i.e. url.ParseQuery over the wire, which percent-decodes both keys and values. Two routes reach the same sink. (a) style deepObject: urlValuesDecoder.DecodeObject lines 661-687 walks every query key matching `^<param>\[`, pulls out every bracket group with FindAllStringSubmatch(key, -1), and joins them into a property path at line 679. (b) the DEFAULT style for query parameters - Parameter.SerializationMethod returns {form, explode:true} when the document sets neither (openapi3/parameter.go:293-302) - where line 650 copies EVERY query key into the property map verbatim, the parameter name not being part of the key at all in that style. Both feed makeObject (line 911), which splits the key on urlDecoderDelimiter (\x1F, line 635) and deepSet()s the resulting path. url.ParseQuery percent-decodes keys, so `%1F` inside a key becomes that delimiter and forges a nested path in route (b) as well; line 916 rejects the delimiter in the VALUE and never checks the KEY. buildResObj (line 972) then reaches `schema.Value.Type.Is("array")` for the array property and calls sliceMapToSlice (line 982). sliceMapToSlice (lines 936-961) runs strconv.Atoi over the map keys, takes max across them against no bound at all, and loops `for i := 0; i <= max; i++ { result = append(result, ...) }` at line 953; buildResObj line 986 then does `make([]any, len(arr))` on what comes back. Sink: two slices of max+1 interface values, 16 bytes each on 64-bit, sized by an integer the client typed into the URL. Concretely, for a query parameter of type object carrying an array property `items`: `?p[items][2147483000]=x` on the deepObject route, and `?items%1F2147483000=x` on the default form route - about thirty bytes either way, asking the allocator for tens of gigabytes twice. Absence of a bound was checked, not assumed: `grep -rn 'maxIndex|MaxIndex|limit|Limit|cap\(|bound' openapi3filter/*.go` returns only an error-code comment and a licence line, and sliceMapToSlice has exactly one caller, so no wrapper bounds it. The x-www-form-urlencoded body decoder reaches the same code through decodeSchemaConstructs -> decodeProperty -> decodeValue (lines 1419-1473), and Encoding.Validate permits deepObject there too (openapi3/encoding.go:145).
findings.impact: One unauthenticated HTTP request of a few dozen bytes makes the server process allocate memory proportional to an integer the attacker chose. On 64-bit the practical outcome is an out-of-memory kill of the whole API process, which Go cannot recover from; under a memory-capped container it is a restart loop. The allocation happens inside request validation, so it lands before the application's handler, before any authorization check, and before any per-route quota the application implements itself.
findings.preconditions: The served document declares a query parameter whose schema resolves to an array under an object - either explicitly with `style: deepObject`, or with the default `style: form, explode: true`, which needs nothing written in the document at all - or an x-www-form-urlencoded request body with an equivalent property. No credential is needed: openapi3filter.ValidateRequest runs decodeStyledParameter before the handler. The attacker does not control the document; that is the one precondition outside their reach and the reason this is high rather than critical.
findings.recommendation: Bound the index before it sizes anything, inside sliceMapToSlice: reject as a ParseError - the same way a non-integer key is already rejected at line 943 - any index that is negative or that exceeds len(m) by more than a small constant, and additionally cap the reconstructed length against schema.MaxItems when the document declares one. Sizing the result from len(m) and filling by index removes the class instead of raising the ceiling: the allocation should be proportional to the bytes received, never to a number found in them. Line 986 needs no separate change once sliceMapToSlice cannot return an oversized slice. Independently, reject the urlDecoderDelimiter byte in the KEY at line 915, not only in the value at line 916, so the default form style cannot forge a nested path at all.
findings.limits: No Go toolchain exists on this host, so the allocation was not observed at runtime; the claim rests on reading the path end to end. It does not establish which of the two allocations fails first, nor the per-element cost on 32-bit builds. It says nothing about deployments that cap request size in front of the service - such a cap does not help, because the payload is short and the amplification lives in the index - though a proxy that rejects square brackets or control bytes in query keys would blunt it.

findings.title: OpenAPI 3.1 validation silently falls back to a validator that enforces none of the 2020-12 keywords

location.component: openapi3: useJSONSchema2020, reached from Schema.VisitJSON whenever the document is OpenAPI 3.1

findings.evidence: openapi3filter turns on the 2020-12 path for every 3.1 document (openapi3filter/validate_request.go:242-244 and 354-356 append EnableJSONSchema2020 when route.Spec.IsOpenAPI31OrLater()). Schema.VisitJSON then routes to useJSONSchema2020 (openapi3/schema.go:1945-1947). useJSONSchema2020 is three lines: build the validator, and `if err != nil { return schema.visitJSON(settings, value) }` - a silent downgrade with no error, no log and no option to make it fail closed. What the downgrade costs is checkable in this tree: grepping the whole value-validation range of schema.go (lines 1942-3000, the visitJSON/visitJSONObject/visitJSONArray/visitJSONString family) for PrefixItems, Contains, PatternProperties, PropertyNames, DependentSchemas, DependentRequired, UnevaluatedItems, UnevaluatedProperties, If, Then and Else returns nothing. Those fields exist only in the struct (schema.go:138-146), in marshalling (614-638), in JSONLookup (880-917), in $ref resolution (1296-1334) and in document-level validation (1444-1484, 1753-1860). So under the fallback, `unevaluatedProperties: false`, `patternProperties`, `propertyNames`, `dependentRequired`, `if/then/else`, `prefixItems` and `contains` are parsed, resolved, document-validated - and then not applied to a single request value. The trigger I can point at is nested $ref: newJSONSchemaValidator starts from json.Marshal(schema) (line 21), and SchemaRef.MarshalYAML returns `&Ref{Ref: ref}` and discards the resolved Value whenever Ref is non-empty (openapi3/refs.go:1049-1054). The one resource handed to the compiler is that schema alone, under https://example.com/schema.json (lines 39-42), so an internal pointer such as `#/components/schemas/Tag` has no `components` member to resolve against and Compile returns an error - which lands on line 207.
findings.impact: An API author who wrote 2020-12 constraints into a 3.1 document believes those constraints gate the request; they do not. `unevaluatedProperties: false` is the 2020-12 way to refuse unexpected properties across composed schemas, so its silent absence reopens the mass-assignment surface it was written to close; `dependentRequired` and `if/then/else` silently stop coupling fields; `propertyNames` and `patternProperties` stop restricting keys. What the attacker gains is the ability to submit shapes the specification forbids - what that is worth depends on the handler behind it, which is why this is medium and not high.
findings.preconditions: An OpenAPI 3.1 document (openapi 3.1.x), validated through openapi3filter, whose schemas both use $ref and rely on at least one 2020-12-only keyword. The attacker controls neither, and nothing in the request is needed to trigger the downgrade - it happens on every validation.
findings.recommendation: Two independent fixes, and the first is the one that matters. (1) Do not fail open: propagate the compile error, or at minimum surface it once per schema through a caller-visible hook, so a document whose 2020-12 constraints cannot be honoured is a startup failure and not a silent runtime downgrade. (2) Make compilation succeed for real documents: marshal the whole component set as additional resources under matching base URIs before compiling, or resolve $ref into the marshalled map, so internal pointers resolve. Separately, either implement the 2020-12-only keywords in the built-in visitJSON path or make Schema.Validate reject a 3.1 document that uses a keyword the fallback cannot enforce - a document that validates but is not enforced is the worst of both.
findings.inference: That jsonschema.Compile actually fails on the marshalled schema. The dangling internal $ref is read from this tree and is unambiguous, but the compiler's behaviour on an unresolvable pointer lives in github.com/santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema/v6, which is not vendored here and which I did not read.
findings.what_would_settle_it: Calling newJSONSchemaValidator on any resolved *Schema that has a nested $ref and printing the returned error, or reading the ref-resolution step of jsonschema/v6's Compiler.Compile. A one-test check would also settle it: assert that a 3.1 document with `unevaluatedProperties: false` plus a $ref rejects an object carrying an unevaluated property.

triage.reason: Whether a given deployment puts a second schema validator in front of kin-openapi is a fact about that deployment and no artifact for it exists inside this repository. FP-08 forbids reading that silence favourably, so this stays UNKNOWN and the finding stays below confirmed.

findings.limits: It does not establish how often compilation fails in the field - only that when it does, nothing says so. It does not enumerate which 2020-12 keywords a specific document depends on. It says nothing about OpenAPI 3.0 documents, where those keywords are rejected outright at document validation (openapi3/schema.go:1444-1484) and the question does not arise.

findings.title: The OpenAPI 3.1 schema is re-marshalled and recompiled from scratch on every validated value

location.component: openapi3: newJSONSchemaValidator, called once per Schema.VisitJSON on 3.1 documents

findings.evidence: useJSONSchema2020 calls newJSONSchemaValidator(schema) on every invocation (line 205), and newJSONSchemaValidator does the whole build each time: json.Marshal of the entire schema (line 21), json.Unmarshal into a map (line 27), a full recursive transformOpenAPIToJSONSchema walk (line 32), jsonschema.NewCompiler(), AddResource and Compile (lines 35-45), the last of which recompiles every regular expression in pattern and patternProperties. There is no cache: `grep -rn 'newJSONSchemaValidator|jsonSchemaValidator'` over the module returns only the declaration, this one call site and the struct - nothing stores or reuses the result, and the compiled validator is discarded when the function returns. The call site above it is per request and per value: openapi3filter appends EnableJSONSchema2020 in ValidateParameter (validate_request.go:242) and in ValidateRequestBody (validate_request.go:354), so an operation with N parameters plus a body pays N+1 full marshal-and-compile cycles per request. The cost is paid even when it is wasted: on the failure path of F-002 the whole build runs, errors, and is thrown away before visitJSON does the real work.
findings.impact: Request-validation CPU is proportional to the size of the schema rather than to the size of the request, so a minimal request against an operation backed by a large component schema costs orders of magnitude more CPU than it costs the attacker to send. A handful of concurrent clients issuing empty-bodied requests can saturate the CPU of a service that looks, from its traffic graph, to be idle. It is availability only - nothing is read, written or bypassed.
findings.preconditions: An OpenAPI 3.1 document served through openapi3filter. No credential and no unusual request content are needed; every validated request pays the cost, and the attacker simply sends more of them.
findings.recommendation: Compile once and reuse. Cache the compiled *jsonschema.Schema on the Schema value - the same shape the pattern cache already uses at openapi3/schema.go:46 with a sync.Map - or build the validator when the document is loaded rather than when a value is validated, which also makes a compile failure a startup error and closes F-002 at the same time.
findings.limits: No measurement was taken - there is no Go toolchain on this host - so the ratio between schema size and per-request CPU is argued from what the code does, not benchmarked. It does not establish a threshold at which a given deployment tips over, and it does not apply to OpenAPI 3.0 documents, which never enter this path.

findings.title: Enabling external $ref resolution grants unbounded local file reads and outbound requests, with no confinement and no timeout
findings.evidence: With Loader.IsExternalRefsAllowed set - which the README's own request-validation quick-start does at README.md:114 - a $ref string from the document becomes a filesystem path or an outbound URL with nothing in between. resolvePath (openapi3/loader.go:307-319) returns an absolute path unchanged when filepath.IsAbs, and otherwise joins it with path.Join after path.Dir, which normalises `..` and therefore walks out of the document's directory. ReadFromFile then calls os.ReadFile(path.Clean(...)) with no base-directory check (loader_uri_reader.go:79-84), and ReadFromHTTP issues a GET to whatever host the ref names (lines 51-69). The loader computes the very value that would confine this and never reads it: `grep -rn 'rootDir|rootLocation'` over the whole module - tests included - returns the two field declarations (loader.go:60-61), the two assignments (loader.go:95 and 191) and nothing else. Zero readers. Two further facets of the same reader: the HTTP client is http.DefaultClient, which has no Timeout and follows redirects, so one ref can hang a goroutine indefinitely or be redirected past any host check a caller thought it had made; and URIMapCache (lines 90-116) stores every fetched body in a map that is never evicted, so a long-lived process that resolves refs from many documents grows without bound. The library's own SECURITY comment (loader.go:41-48) names `$ref: "/etc/passwd"` and `$ref: "http://169.254.169.254/..."` as the consequences, but scopes the warning to a custom ReadFromURIFunc; the default reader behaves the same way once the flag is on, and no allowlist, scheme filter or base-directory API is offered to a caller who legitimately needs multi-file local specs.
findings.impact: A service that parses OpenAPI documents supplied by its users - a spec linter, a gateway that ingests uploaded definitions, a converter, a CI check on a pull request - reads any file its process can read and returns the content inside the resolved document, which is typically rendered back to the submitter; and it issues arbitrary GETs from its own network position, reaching loopback services, internal hosts and cloud metadata. The all-or-nothing flag is the core of it: there is no way to allow `./common/schemas.yaml` without also allowing `/proc/self/environ` and `http://169.254.169.254/`.
findings.preconditions: The consuming application must both accept OpenAPI documents from an untrusted source and set IsExternalRefsAllowed (or install a ReadFromURIFunc that delegates to DefaultReadFromURI, which the field comment already flags). Neither is observable from inside this library. With the flag left at its default of false, loader.go:107-112 rejects every external ref and none of this is reachable.
findings.recommendation: Give the caller a bound it can actually set, rather than one switch. Read the rootDir the loader already computes and refuse a resolved path that escapes it unless the caller opts out; add a scheme and host allowlist consulted by ReadFromHTTP; build ReadFromHTTP's default client with an explicit Timeout and a CheckRedirect that re-applies the allowlist on every hop rather than reusing http.DefaultClient; and either bound URIMapCache or stop making the caching reader the default for long-lived processes, which its own comment says it is not suited to. Until then, document at the IsExternalRefsAllowed field - not only at ReadFromURIFunc - that enabling it on an untrusted document is arbitrary file read and SSRF.
findings.inference: That a deployment exists which feeds attacker-supplied documents to a Loader with external refs enabled. Everything from the flag to the os.ReadFile and the http.Do is read in this tree; who calls it, and with what document, is not visible from inside a library.
findings.what_would_settle_it: Any consumer of this module that calls LoadFromData or LoadFromURI on bytes received over the network while setting IsExternalRefsAllowed - the README quick-start at README.md:114 sets the flag but loads a local file, so it demonstrates the configuration without demonstrating the untrusted input. A canary test settles the mechanism itself: a document containing `$ref: "/etc/hostname"` loaded with the flag on, and the loaded document inspected for the file's content.

triage.reason: The opt-in flag is a real control and its default of false is the reason this is not critical, but FP-05 requires the exposure to be BOUNDED once intended, and behind the flag there is no bound at all: no scheme allowlist, no host allowlist, no base-directory confinement (the rootDir computed at loader.go:95 has zero readers), no client timeout. Following FP-05's own instruction, the finding moves to what sits behind the intended exposure rather than disappearing.

Whether a consuming deployment restricts egress at the network layer, or runs the parser in a sandbox with no filesystem, is configuration outside this repository and no artifact for it arrived. FP-08 refuses to read that silence as a control.

findings.limits: It does not establish that any particular consumer of this library is exposed - that is the named inference. No request was ever issued and no file was ever read as part of this audit. It does not evaluate the ReadFromURIFunc implementations a caller may install instead of the default, which the field comment already covers, and it does not assess whether following redirects can defeat an allowlist a caller writes today, because no allowlist API exists to test.

findings.title: A schema pattern that fails to compile leaves a nil matcher that is then called, panicking under MultiError
findings.evidence: Lines 2654-2666: the compiled matcher is looked up in the global cache, and when it is absent compilePattern is called. On failure the code branches on settings.multiError - `if !settings.multiError { return err }` - and when MultiError is on it appends the error and falls through to `if !cp.MatchString(value)` at line 2666 with the failed matcher. compilePattern returns that matcher unset on the error path (openapi3/schema_pattern.go:16-32): with the default compiler `cp, err = regexp.Compile(...)` assigns a nil *regexp.Regexp into the RegexMatcher interface, so the interface is non-nil, the nil check at line 2657 does not catch it, and MatchString dereferences a nil receiver; with a caller-supplied RegexCompilerFunc that returns (nil, err) the interface itself is nil and the method call panics directly. Both are unrecoverable nil dereferences. MultiError is a one-line opt-in that openapi3filter forwards from its own Options (openapi3filter/validate_request.go:236-238 and 340-342).
findings.impact: Every request that reaches that string schema panics inside validation. Under net/http the per-connection recover turns it into a dropped connection and a 500 rather than a process death, so what the attacker gains beyond an ordinary validation rejection is marginal; where the same validation runs outside an HTTP server goroutine - a worker, a batch validator, a custom transport - the panic is unrecovered and takes the process with it.
findings.preconditions: openapi3filter Options.MultiError (or openapi3.MultiErrors) enabled, and a pattern that fails to compile at request time. Document validation normally catches that first at openapi3/schema.go:1684-1688 - so this needs one of: Validate never called, DisableSchemaPatternValidation set (cmd/validate exposes exactly that as --patterns=false), or a request-time Options.RegexCompiler different from the one Validate used, which is easy since they are two separate knobs (openapi3filter/options.go:29 versus openapi3/validation_options.go:159).
findings.recommendation: Return after appending the error instead of falling through - or guard the call with `if cp == nil`. The multiError branch should collect the compile failure and skip the pattern check, exactly as the non-multiError branch already skips everything by returning.
findings.inference: That a real configuration combines MultiError with a pattern that fails to compile at request-validation time. Each half is a documented, supported setting and the code path between them is read in full; that some deployment holds both at once is argued, not observed.
findings.what_would_settle_it: A unit test that calls Schema.VisitJSON with MultiErrors() on a schema whose Pattern is valid ECMA but invalid RE2 - a lookahead such as `^(?=.*a)` - after loading the document with DisableSchemaPatternValidation. If it panics, the inference closes.

triage.reason: Whether the consuming process runs this validation inside a net/http handler - where the panic is recovered per connection - or in a plain goroutine, where it is fatal, is a property of the caller and no artifact for it exists in this repository.

findings.limits: It does not establish the interface nil-ness argument by execution - no Go toolchain is available - only by reading the assignment in schema_pattern.go. It does not survey which real-world documents carry RE2-incompatible patterns. It says nothing about the concurrency note already carried in schema_pattern.go:15.

findings.title: Neither CI workflow declares permissions, and the job token is exported to steps that fetch and run third-party code at @latest

location.component: GitHub Actions: build-and-test and check-goimports jobs

findings.evidence: Neither .github/workflows/go.yml nor .github/workflows/shellcheck.yml contains a `permissions:` key at any level, so both inherit the repository's default GITHUB_TOKEN permission, which may be read+write. go.yml additionally puts the token into the job environment at line 10 (`GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}`), which makes it visible to every step of build-and-test - including line 59, `go run golang.org/x/tools/go/analysis/passes/modernize/cmd/modernize@latest`, and line 99, the same shape for nilness. The sibling job check-goimports has no env block but does `go install github.com/incu6us/goimports-reviser/v3@latest` (line 202) and then executes it over every file (line 204) after actions/checkout@v6 (line 198); checkout persists the job token into .git/config by default, so third-party code running afterwards can read it from disk even without the env var. Both workflows trigger on `push` as well as `pull_request` (go.yml lines 3-4), and it is the push path that matters: fork pull requests get a read-only token, whereas a push to a branch of the repository itself runs with the repository default.
findings.impact: If any of the three @latest toolchain modules is compromised upstream, the malicious version executes on a runner that has the repository's GITHUB_TOKEN in its environment and in .git/config. With a read+write default that is push access to the repository from CI, which is the standard route from a compromised build tool to a compromised release.
findings.preconditions: The repository's default workflow permission must be read+write, which is the historical default and which cannot be seen from inside the tree; and one of the three unpinned upstreams must be compromised. On fork pull requests the token is read-only regardless, so the exposure is the push path.
findings.recommendation: Add `permissions: contents: read` at the top of both workflows and raise it per job only where a job needs more - nothing in these two workflows writes to the repository. Drop the job-level GITHUB_TOKEN env entirely unless a step demonstrably needs it, and pass `persist-credentials: false` to actions/checkout in any job that then executes third-party code. Fixing F-007 removes the other half.
findings.inference: The repository's default workflow permission setting. It is an organisation or repository console setting, it is not represented anywhere in the tree, and no exported artifact for it was provided.
findings.what_would_settle_it: The repository's Settings > Actions > Workflow permissions value, or an organisation policy export showing the default GITHUB_TOKEN permission. Read-only would reduce this to hardening; read+write confirms it.

triage.reason: The default GITHUB_TOKEN permission for this repository lives in the GitHub console, not in the tree, and no export or written statement about it arrived. FP-08 states plainly that this must be UNKNOWN rather than HOLDS, which is what keeps this finding at probable.

findings.limits: It does not establish the repository's actual default permission - that is the named inference. It does not claim any of the three upstreams is compromised today. It does not cover organisation-level rulesets, required reviews or environment protection, none of which are visible from the tree.

findings.title: No GitHub Action is pinned by commit SHA, three build tools are fetched at @latest, and one action is on an end-of-life major
findings.evidence: Seven `uses:` references across the two workflows, none pinned to a 40-character SHA: actions/setup-go@v6 (go.yml:28 and 200), actions/cache@v3 (go.yml:33), actions/checkout@v6 (go.yml:43 and 198), plus actions/checkout@v2 (shellcheck.yml:12) and ludeeus/action-shellcheck@1.1.0 (shellcheck.yml:15). A git tag is a mutable pointer, so each of these resolves to whatever commit the tag names at run time. Three further references are stronger than a tag and weaker than anything: go.yml:59 and go.yml:99 execute `go run <module>@latest`, and go.yml:202 does `go install github.com/incu6us/goimports-reviser/v3@latest` - `@latest` resolves to whatever version the module proxy serves at that moment, so the code that runs on the runner is chosen after the workflow was reviewed. Two of the tag pins are third-party outside this repository's control (ludeeus/action-shellcheck, incu6us/goimports-reviser); the actions/* ones belong to GitHub rather than to this project's owner. Separately, actions/checkout@v2 in shellcheck.yml is several majors behind and runs on a retired Node runtime.
findings.impact: Every mutable reference is a place where code this project did not review can begin executing in its CI. Combined with F-006 the payload runs beside a repository token. Pinning is the control that turns an upstream tag repoint into a no-op; today it is absent everywhere, and the @latest fetches are the sharpest instance because they cannot even be reasoned about after the fact.
findings.preconditions: None to observe. Exploitation would require an upstream account or tag compromise; none is claimed here, which is why this is hardening rather than an asserted exploit path.
findings.recommendation: Pin all seven `uses:` to a 40-character commit SHA with the human-readable version in a trailing comment, and add a bot (Dependabot or Renovate) to move the SHAs so the pin does not rot. Replace the three @latest module executions with exact versions - the tools can be declared in a tools.go or a separate go.mod so the existing `go mod verify` step covers them and go.sum pins their hashes. Move shellcheck.yml off actions/checkout@v2.

triage.reason: Partially exculpating and worth stating: five of the seven references are actions/* , which is GitHub's own organisation. That is a different perimeter from this project's owner, so FP-06 does not close them, but it does mean the two genuinely third-party references (ludeeus/action-shellcheck, incu6us/goimports-reviser) and the three @latest modules carry most of the risk.

findings.limits: It establishes that pinning is absent, not that anything malicious is being served. It does not check whether a policy outside the tree blocks unpinned actions at merge time - no such artifact was provided, and per FP-08 that absence is not read favourably. It does not review the runner configuration, which is not in the tree; both workflows use GitHub-hosted runners, so the self-hosted half of this class does not apply.

findings.title: The test-fixture cache key escapes its own expression, so one immutable key is shared by every run

location.component: GitHub Actions: actions/cache step in build-and-test

findings.evidence: Line 38 reads `key: suite-\${{ env.APISGURU_COMMIT }}`. The backslash prevents interpolation, so the literal string including the braces becomes the cache key rather than the value of APISGURU_COMMIT declared at line 9. Two consequences follow directly. The key never changes when the pinned fixture commit changes, so a cache written under an older APISGURU_COMMIT is restored for a run that expects a newer one; and because there is only ever one key, the cached content is shared by every branch that can reach it rather than being partitioned per fixture revision. The cached paths are the two APIs-guru fixture directories declared at lines 36-37, which the test suite reads.
findings.impact: The test suite can validate against fixture content that does not correspond to the commit the workflow pins, so a run can pass or fail on the wrong corpus without anything indicating it. It is also the shape a cache-poisoning finding takes: content written into one immutable key by anyone able to run the workflow is later consumed by the build. GitHub's cache scoping keeps fork pull requests out, which is why this stays low.
findings.preconditions: None to observe the key defect. The poisoning half additionally needs push access to a branch whose cache scope the consuming run reads, so it is not reachable by an anonymous outsider.
findings.recommendation: Remove the backslash so the key interpolates - `key: suite-${{ env.APISGURU_COMMIT }}` - and add a hash of the fixture-fetch step's inputs if the fixtures can change without the commit changing.

triage.reason: The primary claim - that the key at .github/workflows/go.yml:38 never interpolates, so one immutable key serves every run - is an integrity defect in what the build consumes and makes no boundary-crossing assertion, so this rule has nothing to answer. For the secondary cache-poisoning reading the second principal would be a repository collaborator, not an anonymous outsider, because GitHub scopes caches so a fork pull request cannot write an entry the base branch reads; that is stated in the impact and is why the severity is low.

The cached data is public API-description fixtures with no security value of their own - but the finding is about what the build consumes, not about the confidentiality of the content, so this rule does not close it.

findings.limits: It does not establish that any stale or poisoned cache has ever been served. It does not examine GitHub's cache-scoping rules beyond the documented fork restriction, which was not verified against a live repository.

findings.title: A credential-shaped string is committed in a vendored test fixture

location.component: test fixture: a vendored public API description

findings.evidence: A distinctive-format scan over all 1667 tracked files - the whole tree, testdata included, for AWS-style access key identifiers, GitHub personal-access-token prefixes, fine-grained PAT prefixes, Anthropic and Slack key formats, Google API keys, GitLab tokens and PEM private-key headers - returned exactly one hit, redacted here as [REDACTED:secret]. It sits inside an `examples.response.value` block of a vendored third-party OpenAPI description, as one query parameter of a pre-signed S3 URL dated 2017 with a one-hour expiry. The matched token is an access key identifier, not a secret access key; no corresponding secret and no private key material appears anywhere in the tree. A second heuristic scan for assignment-shaped credentials outside testdata returned nothing.
findings.impact: None demonstrated. The value is a public identifier inside example data from a published API description, the signature that accompanies it expired in 2017, and the secret half that would make it usable is not present. It is recorded so that the next reader does not repeat the scan and so the hit is not mistaken for an unreported live credential.
findings.recommendation: No rotation is called for. If the project adds secret scanning to CI, add this path to the allowlist with a comment naming it as vendored example data, so the detector's first run does not produce a finding somebody has to triage again.

triage.reason: The value is a literal inside a vendored third-party API description's example block at openapi3/testdata/oai_v3_stoplight.json:29766; it is not derived from anything an attacker supplies and it is not consumed by any code path in this module - testdata is read only by *_test.go.

The matched string is an access key identifier, which is public by design; the secret access key is absent and the accompanying signature carries a 2017 timestamp with a one-hour expiry, so the data has no security value. PRV-01 was not needed: no personal data is involved.

findings.limits: The scan covered the working tree only - git history was out of scope by instruction, so a secret removed from HEAD but still reachable in an earlier commit would not have been found, and SUP-17 was therefore not exercised at all. Detection was by distinctive format plus one assignment-shaped heuristic; a high-entropy secret in an unrecognised format would not have matched.

findings.title: The zip body decoder appends the whole read buffer instead of the bytes actually read
findings.evidence: Line 1637 reads into a fixed 256-byte buffer and captures the count, `n, err := rc.Read(buffer)`; line 1639 then appends the entire buffer, `content = append(content, buffer...)`, and never uses n except to decide whether to append at all. Every short read - the last read of every entry, and every read of an entry smaller than 256 bytes - therefore contributes 256 bytes, of which only n came from the archive and the rest is whatever the previous iteration left behind. The same function also sizes its output from a number the archive declares: line 1623 does `make([]byte, 0, bufferSize*len(zr.File))`, where len(zr.File) is the entry count parsed out of the central directory that arrived in the request body.
findings.impact: Two effects, both bounded. The string handed to schema validation - and therefore to the application - contains bytes that were never in the uploaded archive, so the value validated is not the value received, which is a data-integrity defect in a component whose entire job is to decide what the value is. And an archive full of tiny entries turns each 46-byte central-directory record into 256 bytes of retained output plus 256 bytes of pre-allocated capacity, a roughly five-fold amplification on top of whatever the compression ratio already provides.
findings.preconditions: ZipFileBodyDecoder is exported but not registered by default - init() at lines 1334-1349 does not install it - so a consumer must call RegisterBodyDecoder for a zip media type before any request reaches it. Its doc comment at line 1609 already warns about zip bombs, so a caller who reads it knows about decompression ratio; it says nothing about the buffer defect.
findings.recommendation: Append `buffer[:n]`. Then, since the function is exported for third parties to install, bound it properly: cap the total decompressed size and the entry count against a configurable maximum before allocating, rather than pre-sizing from len(zr.File), and use io.CopyN into a limited writer instead of a hand-rolled read loop.

triage.reason: The function is not behind a build tag and is not test scaffolding - it is an exported symbol of the shipped package, listed in the generated API documentation. What is true is that it is opt-in: init() does not register it, so the path only exists in a consumer that called RegisterBodyDecoder. That narrows the audience, which is reflected in the severity, but it does not remove the path from what ships.

findings.limits: It does not establish that any consumer registers this decoder - init() does not, so the path is opt-in, and that is what bounds the severity to low. It does not determine whether the injected padding can flip a specific schema constraint from reject to accept: the padding lengthens the value, so an anchored pattern or a maxLength would be likelier to reject a legitimate upload than to accept a hostile one. The amplification ratio is derived from the ZIP central-directory record size, not measured.

findings.title: The shipped middleware buffers whole request and response bodies with no cap, and reads the request body twice
findings.evidence: ValidateRequestBody does `io.ReadAll(req.Body)` at line 271 with no limit and then re-seats the bytes as a new body. validateSecurityRequirement does the same thing independently at line 448, and it runs first - ValidateRequest calls the security block at lines 45-59 before the request body block at lines 91-115 - so a request that has both security requirements and a body is fully buffered twice, plus a third copy once decodeBody produces the decoded value. On the response side, Validator.Middleware wraps the writer in either strictResponseWrapper, which buffers the entire response before anything is sent (middleware.go:252-257), or warnResponseWrapper, which tees every byte into a bytes.Buffer even when strict mode is off (middleware.go:195). Neither wrapper has a cap, and neither ValidateRequest nor Middleware installs http.MaxBytesReader. A search for a declared bound found none to enforce: there is no Max*, *Limit or *Size knob anywhere in openapi3filter.
findings.impact: Memory per in-flight request is a small multiple of the request body and, for the shipped middleware, of the response body as well, with no ceiling the library sets. Go's net/http imposes no default request-body limit, so an application that adopts Validator.Middleware and assumes the library validates safely inherits an unbounded buffer on both directions; streaming responses also stop streaming under strict mode. The multiplier is small and the input is proportional to what the attacker actually sends, which is what keeps this a hardening item rather than the amplification of F-001.
findings.preconditions: The application does not itself wrap request bodies in http.MaxBytesReader, and for the response half it uses the library's Validator.Middleware. Both are ordinary configurations - the README's own example calls ValidateRequest directly with no body limit.
findings.recommendation: Read security-requirement and body validation from one buffered copy rather than two - the comment at validate_request.go:441 already contemplates this. Add a configurable maximum body size to Options and enforce it with http.MaxBytesReader (or an io.LimitedReader) before io.ReadAll in both places, defaulting to something finite. In Middleware, cap the response wrapper's buffer and document that strict mode is incompatible with streaming responses.

triage.reason: Whether a proxy, ingress or gateway in front of a given deployment caps request size is configuration outside this repository, and no such artifact arrived. FP-08 forbids treating that as a control, so it is recorded as unknown; unlike F-001, a front-door size cap would genuinely bound this one.

findings.limits: No allocation was measured. It does not establish the exact multiplier, which depends on the decoded value's shape. It does not cover ValidateResponse itself, which was not read. What bounds it to low: the memory consumed is proportional to the bytes the attacker actually sent, so the amplification is a small constant rather than the index-driven blow-up of F-001. It is written down anyway because the library ships an HTTP middleware, and a middleware is where the bound belongs.

findings.title: The middleware's default logger writes the full validation error, which embeds the submitted value and the whole schema
findings.evidence:
The default logFunc installed by NewValidator is `log.Printf("%s: %v", message, err)` (middleware.go:68-70), and Middleware calls it on every rejected request with the validation error itself (line 135) and on every unmatched route with the full request URL (line 124). What that error carries is not a summary: SchemaError.Error() appends "
Schema:
  " followed by the JSON-encoded schema and "
Value:
  " followed by the JSON-encoded offending value (openapi3/schema.go:3120-3131), unless the package-level SchemaErrorDetailsDisabled is set - and it is declared false at openapi3/schema.go:34. RequestError.Error() wraps that verbatim (openapi3filter/errors.go:23-38) and ParseError.Error() likewise carries its Value (openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go:66-82). So a rejected login body, a malformed token in a header parameter, or a personal identifier in a query string is written into the application log by default. The value is embedded as encoded JSON, which escapes newlines, so log-line forging is not reachable this way.
findings.impact: Request content that failed validation - which is exactly the content most likely to be a credential typed into the wrong field, a token, or a personal identifier - lands in the application log at whatever retention and access level that log has. Anyone who can read the logs sees data they were not meant to see. Nothing is disclosed to the requester: the default errFunc writes only a generic string (middleware.go:65-67), so this is a log-side exposure only.
findings.preconditions: The application uses openapi3filter.Validator.Middleware without supplying its own OnLog, and has not set openapi3.SchemaErrorDetailsDisabled. Both are the defaults.
findings.recommendation: Make the shipped default log a stable summary - the route, the parameter or field name and the failing schema keyword - and leave the value out; callers who want it can opt in through OnLog, which already exists for exactly that. Failing that, have Middleware set SchemaErrorDetailsDisabled semantics on the error it hands to logFunc, and say plainly at NewValidator that the default logger records submitted values. Consumers today should pass OnLog with a redacting logger.

triage.reason: This is not debug-only behaviour behind a flag: SchemaErrorDetailsDisabled is initialised to false at openapi3/schema.go:34 and the default logFunc is installed unconditionally by NewValidator, so the shipped default is the verbose one.

findings.limits: It does not establish that any particular deployment logs a real credential; that depends on the API's own fields. It does not assess log retention or access control, which are outside this repository. Two escape hatches exist and are one line each - OnLog, and the documented openapi3.SchemaErrorDetailsDisabled at README.md:253-260 - so a caller who knows about the behaviour can close it; the finding is about the shipped default, which is the part the library owns. It does not cover ValidationErrorEncoder, which puts the same error text into an HTTP response body and would be a disclosure to the requester: that file was read only as far as ConvertErrors and convertBasicRequestError, and the rest of it is in not_read.

findings.title: Two regular expressions are compiled inside the per-query-key loop of the deepObject decoder
findings.evidence: The loop at line 664 iterates over every key in the request's query values. Inside it, line 665 calls regexp.MustCompile on a freshly formatted pattern for each key, and line 669 calls regexp.MustCompile again on a constant pattern for each key that matched. Neither is hoisted: the first depends only on the parameter name, which is fixed for the whole call, and the second depends on nothing at all. The number of iterations is the number of distinct query keys the client sent, which is bounded only by the size of the request line that net/http accepts, so the count of compilations scales with the attacker's URL length rather than with anything about the document.
findings.impact: CPU spent on regular-expression compilation grows linearly with the number of query keys in the request, for a request that costs the attacker only bytes. It is a constant-factor amplifier on the same endpoint as F-001, not a separate class of compromise, and it grants the attacker no capability beyond making the server work harder.
findings.preconditions: The document declares a query parameter with style deepObject, which is what selects this branch. No credential is needed.
findings.recommendation: Hoist the constant pattern at line 669 to a package-level var compiled once, and replace the per-key prefix test at line 665 with a plain strings.HasPrefix(key, param+"[") - the pattern is a QuoteMeta'd literal followed by a bracket, so no regular expression is needed for it at all.

triage.reason: Worth stating because it looks like one: this is NOT a ReDoS. The parameter name is passed through regexp.QuoteMeta at line 665 and the second pattern is a constant lazy group, so neither expression backtracks pathologically. The cost is compilation, not matching.

findings.limits: No timing was measured - there is no Go toolchain here - so the per-compilation cost, and therefore the request rate at which this matters, is argued rather than benchmarked. It does not establish the maximum number of query keys a given net/http configuration accepts. It grants an attacker nothing beyond extra server CPU on an endpoint that already carries F-001, which is what bounds it to low.

findings.title: YAML request bodies are decoded with no declared limit on alias expansion

location.component: openapi3filter: YamlBodyDecoder, registered by default for application/yaml and application/x-yaml

findings.evidence: init() registers YamlBodyDecoder for both application/yaml and application/x-yaml (lines 1344-1345), so any operation whose requestBody content names either media type will decode an attacker's YAML. The decoder is `yaml.NewDecoder(body).Decode(&value)` against github.com/oasdiff/yaml3 (import at line 22) with no decoder options, no size limit and no depth or expansion setting - the whole function is five lines. Nested-alias expansion (the billion-laughs shape) is the classic amplifier for this decoder family, and nothing in this repository bounds it: the caller passes an unbounded io.Reader and reads whatever the decoder produces into `any`.
findings.impact: If the decoder does not itself cap alias expansion, a small YAML body expands into an arbitrarily large in-memory value before any schema constraint is consulted, since decoding happens before VisitJSON. If it does cap it, there is no impact at all - which is exactly why this is reported at low confidence rather than asserted.
findings.preconditions: An operation that declares application/yaml or application/x-yaml in its requestBody content. No credential is needed.
findings.recommendation: Do not leave it to the dependency: wrap the body in an io.LimitedReader sized from the same request-body maximum recommended in F-011 before handing it to the YAML decoder, and pin the expansion behaviour with a regression test that feeds a nested-alias document and asserts it is rejected. That test is worth having whether or not the dependency currently protects itself, because it turns a dependency property into a checked property.
findings.inference: Whether github.com/oasdiff/yaml3 caps alias expansion. It is a fork of go-yaml v3, which added such a cap, but the dependency is not vendored in this tree, I did not read its source, and by instruction I consulted no upstream repository or advisory database. I can point at the absence of any bound in kin-openapi's own code; I cannot point at the presence or absence of one below it.
findings.what_would_settle_it: Reading aliasDepth / alias-ratio handling in the decoder of github.com/oasdiff/yaml3, or posting a nested-alias YAML body to an endpoint whose requestBody declares application/yaml and observing the process's memory.

triage.reason: The compensating control, if it exists, lives inside github.com/oasdiff/yaml3, which is not vendored in this tree and which I did not read. Per the corpus rule that a dismissal must name the line of the control, I cannot claim this HOLDS - naming a cap I have not seen would be the exact failure mode the artifact spec warns about - so it stays UNKNOWN and the finding stays probable.

The sink parses rather than evaluates - Decode targets `any`, so there is no type-instantiation or code-execution deserialization risk here, and no gadget class applies. What remains is the expansion cost alone, which is why the severity is low.

findings.limits: This is the weakest claim in the artifact and is written as such. It establishes only that kin-openapi imposes no bound of its own on YAML decoding; it establishes nothing about the dependency, and it must not be read as an assertion that the dependency is vulnerable. No dependency advisory was consulted, by instruction.

ruled_out.where: Not applicable to this module and therefore not exercised. openapi3filter never decides identity: validateSecurityRequirement (openapi3filter/validate_request.go:419-500) resolves the named security scheme and delegates to a caller-supplied AuthenticationFunc, returning ErrAuthenticationServiceMissing when none is set. No token is parsed, no signature is verified and no session is created anywhere in the module.

ruled_out.class: Security-requirement evaluation order and empty-requirement handling
ruled_out.where: Read in full at openapi3filter/validate_request.go:45-59 and 397-416. ValidateRequest falls back to the document-level security when the operation declares none, ValidateSecurityRequirements returns nil only for a genuinely empty requirement list - which is the specification's own way of marking an operation public - and it returns success on the first requirement that passes while requiring every scheme within a requirement to pass. That is the semantics OAS 3 defines. No bypass was found on this path; the bound is that the AuthenticationFunc itself was not reviewed because it belongs to the caller.

ruled_out.class: Content-Type confusion leading to skipped body validation
ruled_out.where: Traced end to end for case variation, absent headers and parameterised media types. Content.Get (openapi3/content.go:64-105) and the bodyDecoders lookup (openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go:1313) are both case-sensitive, but every mismatch path terminates in an error rather than in skipped validation: a media type with no declared content returns a RequestError at validate_request.go:311, and a media type with no registered decoder returns a KindUnsupportedFormat ParseError at req_resp_decoder.go:1322. An absent Content-Type resolves to the empty string and follows the same two paths. It fails closed. The bound is that Content.Get's wildcard fallback was reasoned about, not fuzzed.

ruled_out.class: SQL, ORM, NoSQL and OS command injection
ruled_out.where: The module has no data layer and executes no subprocess: greps across all non-test Go sources find no database/sql, no ORM import, and no os/exec, syscall.Exec or shell invocation. The only interpreters reached are encoding/json, the YAML decoder and regexp. Nothing to inject into.

ruled_out.class: Ref-cycle recursion and schema-graph recursion in the loader
ruled_out.where: Every resolver in openapi3/loader.go guards recursion with shouldVisitRef (line 386), which returns false when the ref string is already in visitedRefs and queues a backtrack callback instead of recursing; visitRef and unvisitRef maintain that set around each descent. Schema.validate carries independent protection via slices.Contains(stack, schema) at openapi3/schema.go:1397. Non-ref recursion is bounded by document nesting, which encoding/json's own nesting limit bounds first. Checked on the schema, path-item, header, parameter, security-scheme, example, callback and link resolvers; the openapi2 loader was not read.

ruled_out.class: Path traversal from request path parameters into the object decoder
ruled_out.where: The delimiter-forging trick that widens F-001 was tested against the path-parameter route and does not reach it: the gorilla/mux router is built with UseEncodedPath (routers/gorillamux/router.go:57), so match.Vars carry percent-encoded segments and a `%1F` in the path stays three literal characters rather than becoming the urlDecoderDelimiter byte. Query keys, which url.ParseQuery does decode, are the reachable route and are reported in F-001. No filesystem sink is reached from any request parameter in this module at all - the only os.ReadFile is in the document loader, covered by F-004.

Not run. The engagement forbids reading .git - history, diffs, tags and branches are out of scope - so only the working tree was scanned. A secret removed from HEAD but still present in an earlier commit would not have been detected. What would unblock it: authorization to run a history scan over the pack files, or an exported scan result from the maintainers.

ruled_out.class: Known vulnerabilities in pinned dependency versions
ruled_out.where: Not run, by instruction: no advisory database, upstream repository, issue tracker or version comparison was consulted, and no Go toolchain exists on this host to run govulncheck. go.mod and go.sum were read for structure only - seven direct and seven indirect modules, all pinned to exact versions with hashes in go.sum. This artifact therefore makes no claim, in either direction, about known vulnerabilities in gorilla/mux v1.8.0, oasdiff/yaml3 v0.0.14, santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema/v6 v6.0.2 or any other pinned version. What would unblock it: authorization to run govulncheck or to query an advisory source.

ruled_out.class: Static analysis of the Go sources
ruled_out.where: No Go toolchain is installed on this host - `go version` reports command not found - so go vet, the nilness pass, staticcheck, the race detector and the project's own test suite were all unavailable. Every finding here is from reading. Note that the project's CI does run go vet, nilness and -race on three specific tests (.github/workflows/go.yml:56, 71-79, 99), so some of that coverage exists upstream; none of it was reproduced here.

ruled_out.class: Prompt injection, agent tooling and LLM data flows
ruled_out.where: No LLM surface exists in the target: no model client, no agent framework, no MCP configuration, no prompt template, and no CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md or .cursor/rules inside the scope. The ai-safety pack was not staffed and not loaded. Worth recording explicitly because AI-22 treats audited content as data: nothing in this tree attempted to address instructions to the auditor, and none was followed.
